#5358. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1411 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1411 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.
  • Sources indicate that A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models.
  • In a recent development, GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

Sources indicate that A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

In a recent development, GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That blueprint is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

According to recent reports, better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It notes nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

According to recent reports, we wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

Recent findings suggest that the short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:.

According to recent reports, here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

It has been revealed that this is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

Two design choices shaped the work:.

In a recent development, we compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

Recent findings suggest that all numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

Recent findings suggest that no single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

It has been revealed that A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That indicates nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Recent findings suggest that linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

It has been revealed that gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

It has been revealed that one caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:.

Recent findings suggest that up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Sources indicate that out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

In a recent development, the full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

An axiomatic foundation for optimized certainty equivalents

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (163 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.22119v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Optimized Certainty Equivalents (OCEs) are an vital class of risk measures for optimization and risk management that includes the Mean--Variance criterion, Expected Shortfall, the Entropic Risk Measure, and expectation. Despite their importance, economic axioms have not characterized OCEs. We propose a new axiom called Fair-Coin Compensation, which characterizes OCEs together with Strong Risk Aversion and Normalization. We interpret Fair-Coin Compensation through the fair assignment of two losses by a coin toss: transfers between two participants can remove the additional risk created by the random assignment. Adding further axioms yields sharper characterizations. Monotonicity yields standard OCEs; Positive Homogeneity, together with Prudence, yields Expected Shortfall; and Fair-Coin Independence yields the Entropic Risk Measure. We also axiomatize the Mean--Variance criterion using our novel axiom of Equal-Mean Randomization, which states that random assignment of two losses with the same expected value does not produce a risk measure above the average of their risk measures.

DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles.
  • The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window.
  • Industry observers note that we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:.

The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

Industry observers note that we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:.

Industry observers note that the model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

In a recent development, daisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Recent findings suggest that scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

Recent findings suggest that we built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

We selected tasks using three criteria:.

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

It has been revealed that 57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

According to recent reports, 2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Recent findings suggest that stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

According to recent reports, every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

It has been revealed that the service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Recent findings suggest that cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

According to recent reports, we thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

arXiv:2611.21897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study examines thirty equity--bond and multi-asset exchange-traded funds (ETFs) listed in the United States, Canada, and Australia using daily U.S.-dollar returns over 2020--2024. A rolling-window framework compares minimum-variance and Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) portfolio optimization under long-only and long--short constraints against an equally weighted benchmark. Performance is assessed using risk-adjusted measures, downside risk, extreme-tail estimation, and conditional volatility models. Optimized portfolios exhibit lower empirical VaR and CVaR than the benchmark, with long--short strategies generally providing greater downside-risk reduction. However, the equally weighted benchmark achieves the highest reported Sharpe, Sortino, and Rachev ratios. GARCH and FIGARCH comparisons favor GARCH based on information criteria. A historically estimated Normal Inverse Gaussian model further generates European option prices and model-implied volatility surfaces under a martingale-corrected pricing specification. The findings highlight trade-offs between risk reduction, risk-adjusted performance, and practical implementation costs.

Who sees the sea? Sea-view potential by fa\c{c}ade and floor from cadastral LoD1 models on the Costa del Sol

📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21672v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Views are among the most valued and least measured attributes of a home. We present an open-data method that estimates the sea-view potential of every free fa\c{c}ade of every residential building at three floors (ground, middle and top; other floors take the nearest of them), from cadastral footprints with floor counts and a national terrain model. Run for 158,060 buildings of 21 municipalities on Spain's Costa del Sol in under an hour on two cores, it finds that 52 % of buildings see some sea from their top floor and 36 % have an open view (20{\deg} or more). Traced over a LiDAR surface in a pilot, scores agree with the model's inside cadastral footprints (96.7 % of viewpoints in the same class at 20{\deg}), but structures the cadastre does not record lower the sea seen from the top floor by 6.1--9.0{\deg} on average. Against the photographs of 93 homes for sale, labelled blind by AI models of two developers with ties decided by the author, the score has an AUC of 0.80 (95 % CI 0.70--0.89; 0.81 against the first-round labels); at 20{\deg} it is sensitive (0.90) but not specific (0.45). Dwelling figures depend on how dwellings are allocated to fa\c{c}ades and floors: 42 % of dwellings are on a floor with open-view potential under the main rule, and 12--45 % across the allocation, geometry and vegetation scenarios tested. As an application, higher-income census sections tend to have more modelled view potential within municipalities, with uncertain size and fragile inference (about two effective clusters); on terrain alone the difference largely disappears. Code and fa\c{c}ade-level data reproduce the main results.

Amazon VPC, AWS Transit Gateway, and AWS Cloud WAN now offer a 99.999% availability SLA for cross-Region traffic

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (394 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that AWS now offers a 99.999% availability service level agreement (SLA) for cross-Region traffic over Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) cross-Region peering, AWS Transit Gateway, and AWS Cloud WAN, with a upcoming capability called Multipath Resilience.
  • The AWS backbone is highly resilient and connects Regions over physically diverse fiber paths.
  • It has been revealed that now, when you turn on Multipath Resilience for a cross-Region VPC peering connection, cross-Region Transit Gateway peering attachment, or cross-Region traffic on Cloud WAN, the network sends copies of each packet across physically diverse paths.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that AWS now offers a 99.999% availability service level agreement (SLA) for cross-Region traffic over Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) cross-Region peering, AWS Transit Gateway, and AWS Cloud WAN, with a upcoming capability called Multipath Resilience. Multipath Resilience makes it easier to improve the resilience of mission-critical applications that send traffic across Regions, such as payment processing, financial trading, telephony, and live media streaming.

The AWS backbone is highly resilient and connects Regions over physically diverse fiber paths. When a path fails, such as during a fiber cut, the network's automatic sub-second rerouting moves traffic to a healthy path. In the rare event that such mechanisms do not resolve the matter in a timely manner, such as when there's a partial degradation, it might take minutes for connectivity to be reestablished. Some applications, such as payment processing, financial trading, telephony, and live media streaming, can't tolerate single-digit seconds interruptions, let alone minutes of unavailability. Until now, customers running these applications relied on workarounds, including modifying their applications and operating systems to split a single connection into multiple connections, or replicating data into every Region to avoid cross-Region calls. These workarounds add complexity and don't always work, because applications can't control which network paths their traffic takes.

It has been revealed that now, when you turn on Multipath Resilience for a cross-Region VPC peering connection, cross-Region Transit Gateway peering attachment, or cross-Region traffic on Cloud WAN, the network sends copies of each packet across physically diverse paths. It delivers whichever copy reaches your resources in the destination Region first and discards the duplicates. If one path drops packets, a copy is already in flight on another path, so your applications stay connected without waiting for the network protocols to reroute. Multipath Resilience moves this work out of your applications and into the network. Your applications keep using a single connection, with no changes to application code or operating systems, and no need to duplicate data to keep calls within a single Region.

Sources indicate that multipath Resilience is now generally available in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), and Europe (Ireland).

It has been revealed that to learn more, visit the Multipath Resilience documentation. For SLA details, visit the Multipath Resilience SLA. For pricing, visit the Amazon VPC pricing page.

Recent findings suggest that today, AWS confirms the general availability of OpenAI GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol on Amazon Bedrock. GPT-6.2 Astra brings frontier-level reasoning and judgment to your most ambitious work, including complex business problems, demanding research, and advanced coding and agentic workflows. Astra also includes an Ultrafast mode for latency-sensitive applications that need fast responses. GPT-6.2 Sol is designed for recurring coding, agentic, and professional workflows with clear outcomes, where speed and cost per task matter.

Use GPT-6.2 Astra for challenging work that calls for expert judgment and a finished deliverable, such as reconciling competing inputs, investigating complex codebases, reasoning across text and images, and creating professional artifacts. Select ultrafast mode for Astra for interactive coding assistants, real-time agents, and customer-facing applications where latency shapes the customer experience. Use GPT-6.2 Sol for recurring, high-volume work with verifiable outcomes, such as implementing and debugging software, analyzing documents and data, and automating multistep workflows. Established AWS controls help you secure workloads, govern access, and audit model invocation activity.

You can get started in the Amazon Bedrock console or programmatically through supported Amazon Bedrock APIs. For information about supported AWS Regions, endpoints, APIs, features, inference profiles and pricing, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation.
